extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and research-integrity professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying manuscripts that may have been created, manipulated, or sold by commercial 'paper mills' and deciding when to investigate, correct the record, or retract. Includes signs to flag, procedural safeguards (e.g., giving authors a chance to respond), and recommended publisher practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article created/manipulated/sold by a commercial entity (paper mill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grounds for retraction when an investigation indicates that some papers may have been created, manipulated, and/or sold by a commercial entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notice language used by IOP: 'This article has been retracted by IOP Publishing following an allegation that raises concerns this article may have been created, manipulated, and/or sold by a commercial entity.' The publisher analyses articles for indicators of illegitimacy and will retract when there are enough indicators to cause serious doubts over the legitimacy of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: No evidence that reliable peer review was conducted
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of reliable peer review on an article is a basis for retraction or serious concern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices state: 'IOP Publishing has seen no evidence that reliable peer review was conducted on this article, despite the clear standards expected of and communicated to conference organisers.' Absence of documented, reliable peer review is a red flag for manipulated/publication-process-compromised papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarities across multiple papers indicating a single source/network
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable similarities among a number of papers (textual, structural, data, or other patterns) that point to a network of content being created by one source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whistleblowers/sleuths may notice similarities; such patterns suggest papers were produced by a single commercial source even if multiple different authors are listed. Publishers should investigate clusters of similar papers as potential paper-mill output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic manipulation of the publication process (including citation manipulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of coordinated manipulation of submission/review/publication workflows or of citation patterns is a criterion for concern and possible retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IOP previously retracted papers after an 'investigation has uncovered evidence of systematic manipulation of the publication process and considerable citation manipulation.' Such findings justify large-scale corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must be given opportunity to present evidence of genuine authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Before finalizing retraction, authors should be offered the chance to present evidence they were the original and genuine creators of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices note authors 'have been given opportunity to present evidence' but may retract if no responsive evidence is received. This is a procedural fairness step in the retraction process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of COPE criteria for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE) criteria to determine when retraction is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IOP states they 'don’t shy away from retracting papers that meet the Committee for Publication Ethics (COPE) criteria for retraction' — implying formal adherence to COPE guidance when deciding to correct the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting the record to protect readers and downstream uses (including AI/text-mining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retracting or correcting unreliable papers is essential to prevent readers and automated systems from building on and propagating false or manipulated findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabanac and Labbé: 'Correcting the record is of utmost importance to prevent readers and AIs (performing text mining for literature-based discovery) from building on unreliable papers and spreading errors.' This motivates proactive correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishers and reviewers should prioritise filtering out problematic/fraudulent papers upfront
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventative screening and filtering of submissions to block paper-mill productions should be a top priority for publishers and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article asserts: 'Filtering out problematic/fraudulent papers upfront should be publishers’ and reviewers’ top priority to block paper mill productions.' Emphasises upstream defenses rather than solely post-publication corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source intelligence from PubPeer and post-publication peer-review platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should gather and act on intelligence from PubPeer and other post-publication peer review platforms as part of detecting problematic papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabanac and Labbé suggest publishers 'should source intelligence from PubPeer and other post-publication peer review platforms (even more).' Dedicated sleuth reports on these platforms are valuable red flags to investigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of independent sleuths and whistleblowers as detection triggers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports from independent investigators, sleuths, or named whistleblowers are legitimate and valuable sources for initiating investigations into suspect publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IOP was alerted by an independent whistle-blower (named) and acknowledges the contribution of 'dedicated sleuths' who 'contribute valuable reports pro bono.' Such reports should be treated as signals warranting further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publicly share detailed detection signals to avoid aiding perpetrators
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should avoid revealing the specific signals or checks they use to detect fraudulent papers, to prevent paper mills from learning how to evade detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IOP Publishing: 'We don’t publicly share the signals that cause us to believe articles are not the genuine work of the authors, as not to reveal too much information to the perpetrators, effectively handing them a “cheat sheet” to avoid being caught in the future.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of systematic screening tools (e.g., Problematic Paper Screener)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing automated or semi-automated screening tools and specialized methods can help identify problematic papers at scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabanac and Labbé, creators of the Problematic Paper Screener, endorse using clever methods and tools to expose fraud; such tooling helps 'depollute the scientific literature' when applied by publishers and investigators.
